Ahobilam Temples
------------------------------------------
Ahobilam is a rare क्षेत्र or place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, specially devoted to the god नरसिṁह.
It is situated near the Rudravaram village in the Nallamalai range of hills of Andhra Pradesh. The distance from Kadapa (or Cuddapah) is 112 kms. (70 miles).
It has two main temples, called in the local language (Telugu) as ‘Diguva Ahobilam’ and ‘Yeguva Ahobilam’.
According to the local legends this hill was once the palace of the demon king हिरण्यकशिपु, wherein, Lord विष्णु emerged out of a pillar in the form of नरसिṁह (man-lion) and killed him. It is this palace that gradually became a hill over thousands of years.
Great sages like वसिष्ठ and गोभिल as also गरुड (the Eagle-mount of विष्णु) are said to have worshipped the Lord नरसिṁह here.
At Yeguva Ahobilam, above the hill, the shrine is small. It is situated in the valley of two high hills and on the bank of the river Bhavanāśinī. The Svayambhū or self-manifested image of नरसिṁह is in a small rock-cut cave (or rather a hollow). By its side there is another small cave housing the image लक्ष्मी, locally known as Ceñcu (Chenchu). The story goes that after नरसिṁह killed हिरण्यकशिपु he continued to stay there forgetting his spouse लक्ष्मी who was languishing in वैकुण्ठ. So Lakṣṁi managed to be born as the beautiful daughter of the chief of the Chenchu tribe (a tribe living in hills and forests). In her youth, she was seen by नरसिṁह who fell in love with her and married her.
The image of नरसिṁह has ten bāhus or arms. Six arms are engaged in killing the demon. Two are holding the शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus). The last two are wearing divine weapons. At his feet is standing the boy-devotee प्रह्लाद.
The temple complex is fairly big. There are quite a few maṇḍapas (pillared structures) out of which one is known as ‘Nūrukāḷḷa-maṇḍapamu’ (the ‘hundred pillered maṇḍpa’). Water of the Bhava-nāśinī river is led into the temple kitchen through pipe-like devices in the rock.
Near this temple, upon one of the precipitous sides of a deep and dangerous ravine, is an iron pillar. If barren women can manage to go round it, they are believed to be blessed with children in course of time.
This temple is said to have been visited by Rāmānuja (A.

-1533)
Tirumaṅgai Āḷvār (8th cent. A. D.) also visited this temple as can be surmised by the reference to it in his poems.
The sixth pontiff of the अहोबिल मठ (See AHOBILA MAṬHA for details.), Parāṅkuśa Yatīndra, is reputed to have had the vision of the deity here and disappered into the cave.
There are nine temples of नरसिṁह spread over the entire region. Hence it is called ‘Nava-Nārasiṁha-क्षेत्र’.
Out of these, three are situated at (Diguva Abohilam) the foot of the hills. They are: भार्गव नरसिṁह; Yogānanda नरसिṁह, and Chatrapaṭa नरसिṁह.
The other six, above the hills, are: Kārañja नरसिṁह; Abohila नरसिṁह (the main deity); Kroḍākāra (or Varāha) नरसिṁह; Mālola नरसिṁह; Jvālā नरसिṁह; Pāvana नरसिṁह.
Apart from these nine deities, there is the tenth deity known as ‘Prahlāda-Varada-नरसिṁह’. This is the god at the main temple in Diguva Ahobilam.
The small river Bhavanāśinī, consi-dered as equal to गङ्गा, flows on these hills. This is said to be the river in which Lord नरसिṁह washed his blood-stained hands after killing the demon हिरण्यकशिपु.
Thirteen rivulets, all being tributaries of Bhavanāśinī, are also found on the hills. Some of them are: नरसिṁह-tīrtha; रामतीर्थ; Śaṅkaratīrtha; Varāhatīrtha and Bhairavatīrtha.
The Diguva Ahobilam temple was ransacked by muslim marauders in A.

. Two generals of the Vijayanagar Empire came here, drove away the enemies and restored the original glory. In memory of this victory, a stone pillar called ‘Jayastambha’ was erected in front of the temple which can be seen even today.
About 20 inscriptions dating from the 14th to the 16th centuries have been found here.
The main festivals celebrated in the temples are: Brahmostsava (the annual festival); नरसिṁह Jayantī; दसरा.
There is also another festival called ‘Parvata-festival’. During this period the उत्सव-mūrti (festival image) is taken round the nearby villages (about 50) for 45 days. This is an occasion of great joy and mirth for the village folks.
See also NARASIṀHA.

Ahobila Maṭha
(‘the Ahobila Monastery’)
------------------------------------------
Maṭhas (monasteries) and maṭhādhi-patis (pontiffs) have played a very signi-ficant role in spreading, consolidating and preserving Hindu religion and culture among the masses. A मठ is more than just a monastery, though the residence of the monk or मोन्क्स् is an important and integral part of the same. A temple, an auditorium and a school for the pursuit of religious and philosophical studies exist invariably in any मठ of repute.
Among the more well-known of such maṭhas, the अहोबिल मठ of the Śrī-vaiṣṇavas which follows the Viśiṣṭādvaita school of philosophy propagated by Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) and others has carved out an important place for itself.
Ahobila is an important place of पिल्ग्रिमगे situated in the Vedācala hill range of the Eastern ghats. It is about 23 kilometers (15 miles) from Āḷḷagaḍḍa, in the Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh. When Mahāviṣṇu manifested himself in the form of नरसिṁह (‘man-lion’) and killed the demon हिरण्यकशिपु with his bare hands, the gods are said to have exclaimed ‘aho! balam!’ (‘Wonderful is the strength!’). Since many stone icons of this नरसिṁह aspect are found in the several ‘bilas’ or caves of this place, the place itself has been named ‘Aho-bilam.’
The founder-pontiff of the अहोबिल मठ was Ādivaṇa-Śaṭhagopa-Yatīndra-Mahādeśikan, known as श्रीनिवास in his premonastic days. Born in A.

in Tirunārāyaṇapura (the present Melkote near the Mysore City of Karnataka) and brought up in a holy and scholarly atmosphere, श्रीनिवास was commanded in a vision by Lord नरसिṁह to go to Ahobila and take सṁन्यास (monastic order). Accordingly he went there and was initiated into सṁन्यास by an old monk who appeared there mysteriously, enlightened him about the mission of his life and disappeared. Acting as the servant of Lord लक्ष्मी-Nṛsiṁha whose image he used to carry, शठकोप established a chain of maṭhas wherein he arranged for the study of the works of Rāmānuja and वेदान्त देशिक. He is said to have accorded some privileges to the lower classes in the temples he built at Kadiri (Andhra Pradesh) and elsewhere. He passed away in A.

.
Among his successors, called Jīyars, mention may be made of the 6th, Parāṅ-कुश (A.
-1513) who was reputed to have acquired extraordinary yogic powers, the 33rd, Śaṭhagopa (the VI) (A.
-1879) who converted robbers into devotees, the 38th, श्रीनिवास (A.
-1909) who proved to be an excellent administrator, and the 40th, रङ्गनाथ (the IV) (A.

-1923) who was a rare combination of scholarship and yogic powers.
Unlike the other maṭhas, the अहोबिल मठ does not have a Headquarters. It moves along with the Jīyar, the pontiff. The deity worshipped is known as Mālola लक्ष्मी-Nṛsiṁha, the image being of solid gold. Only the devotees of the Vaḍagalai (‘Northern’) sect of Śrīvaiṣṇavas are disciples and followers of this मठ.
See also ŚRĪVAIṢṆAVISM.
